Example: Two SCARA fingers grasping a box

scenes.title: Why Hands
scenes.brief: Split screen. Left: a long slate arm with orange joints and a tiny pink pen tip trying to trace a gold star; joint jitter (purple) is amplified by the long links so the trace wobbles. Right: the same arm frozen, with a small three-finger hand doing the tracing; the wobble shrinks (readout: trace error bar, coral, drops). Next beat: a parallel-jaw gripper tries a cube, a pyramid and a ball; only the cube gets a lime ✓. Then the hand is exploded into its fingers, each drawn as a mini robot arm with orange joints. Final beat: two gold wish-icons (🛡️ resist any shove, 🔀 move any way) light up as later scenes are unlocked, with a chapter road map of emoji tiles.

scenes.title: Contact Types
scenes.brief: A blue object with a teal contact dot; a small RGB frame sits on the dot with z (blue) poking inward along the surface normal. The learner drags an orange finger-force arrow. Frictionless mode: only the inward normal component survives (lime); any pull or sideways part flashes coral. Friction mode: a translucent lime ice-cream cone of half-angle atan μ sits on the dot; a μ slider widens/narrows it; arrows inside are lime and hold, arrows outside turn coral and the finger slides away. Soft-finger mode adds a curling orange torque ring about the normal with its own small lime band |τ| ≤ γ·fn. Last beat: a matrix B (columns as arrows) times a vector in the cone builds the wrench; three contact cards (point, friction, soft) swap B and the cone.

scenes.title: Grasp Map
beats: 🔁 carry a push to the center
📦 two soft fingers on a box
scenes.brief: A blue object with a gold dot at its center of mass. Each teal contact has a pushing arrow; a ghost copy of the arrow slides to the center and grows a curling torque arrow (p × f), showing the wrench transform Adᵀ. With several fingers, the center wrenches stack tip-to-tail into one net wrench (pink). A matrix panel shows G built column by column, each column glowing when its finger is selected. Beat 3: a 3D box pinched by two soft fingers; the 6×8 G appears with blocks colored per finger. Beat 4: a 2D rectangle pinched from left and right, the 3×4 G, with the wrench (fx, fy, τ) shown as a point in a 3D plot.

scenes.title: Force Closure
beats: 🔁 proof back: two pushes make a squeeze
scenes.brief: A blue object held by teal contacts with lime friction cones. The learner drags a coral "external shove" wrench arrow (and a torque dial) anywhere; the solver finds finger forces inside the cones whose net wrench (pink) is exactly opposite; if none exist the object flies off and a coral 🚫 flashes. A gold "squeeze" slider adds the internal force f_N: fingers press harder toward each other, the net wrench meter stays at zero, but every finger arrow tilts toward the middle of its cone. Proof staircase: an arbitrary (coral, out-of-cone) solution f′ plus α·f_N, with α growing, until every arrow turns lime; then the converse: one interior push plus the push that cancels it add to an interior squeeze.

scenes.title: Positive Span
scenes.brief: Arrows (columns of G) from the origin in 2D, then in 3D (fx, fy, τ). Weight sliders accept only positive values; the reachable region (lime) fills in as positive mixes. A rubber-band polygon/polyhedron (convex hull, blue translucent) wraps the arrow tips; a gold origin dot is either strictly inside (lime glow, closure) or outside/on the skin (coral). A slate plane through the origin can be rotated by the learner: if all arrow tips fall on one side, the plane is a separating wall and lights coral (closure fails). Beat 5 auto-builds candidate walls perpendicular to pairs of columns and shows the sign pattern of the dot products as ±chips. Beat 6 replaces each friction cone by its two (2D) or n (3D pyramid) edge rays and reuses the same test.

scenes.title: How Many Fingers
scenes.brief: An object outline (polygon, disk, ellipse; 3D: cube, sphere). The learner clicks to place frictionless contacts; each adds a wrench arrow (n, p×n) in a 3D wrench plot with a convex-hull bubble around the tips. A counter shows k vs. the bounds p+1 and 2p as orange ticks. For the disk/sphere every normal passes through the center so all torque parts are zero: the bubble is flat and the origin never gets inside (coral 🚫) no matter how many contacts. Beat 3: try to positively span the plane with 2 arrows: the gold target −(v1+v2) is always unreachable. Beat 4: a big cloud of arrows is pruned down to at most 2p that still enclose the origin. Final beat: a table of emoji rows (plane/space × frictionless/friction/soft) filled in with counts.

scenes.title: Antipodal Grasp
scenes.brief: A polygon (default: equilateral triangle) with two draggable teal contact dots on its edges; each shows a lime V friction cone (μ slider). A dashed gold line joins the dots; when it lies inside both cones it turns lime and the object can be lifted and shaken without slipping; otherwise coral. Beat 2 shows the four inequality chips A–D (cross products of cone edges with the connecting line) as ± signs. Beat 3: a unit square plot (position along edge 1 × position along edge 2), with the force-closure region shaded lime and the largest inscribed square in gold; moving a point in the square moves the dots on the triangle. Beat 4: same idea on a 3D box with soft fingers and on a curved blob where the boundary curves are found by root-finding.

scenes.title: Grasp Constraint
beats: 🤲 hand Jacobian: Jh θ̇ = Gᵀ V
scenes.brief: Two planar (then 3D) fingers with orange joints on a slate palm hold a blue object at teal contacts. Each contact shows two tiny frames: Fᵢ (pink, rides the fingertip) and Cᵢ (teal, rides the object). The learner drags joint sliders or the object; the relative twist between Fᵢ and Cᵢ is drawn as arrows split into lime (free, e.g. rolling about the contact) and coral (forbidden: exactly the directions where the contact can push, Bᵀ V = 0). A chain-of-frames ribbon S→F→C→O→P animates the adjoint composition. Final beat: the block-diagonal Jh panel and Gᵀ panel; moving the object with the mouse solves for θ̇ live (pinv) and the fingers follow; a residual meter shows Jh θ̇ − Gᵀ V stays 0.

scenes.title: Grasp Properties
scenes.brief: Two-finger planar hand around a blue object. A gold target twist of the object (drag a ghost) is tested against range(Jh): if every target can be met the 🔀 badge is lime, otherwise the unreachable directions flash coral. A null-space slider moves fingers without moving the object (internal motion, orange ghost trail). A 2×3 diagram (rows: velocity/force; columns: joints, contacts, object) with arrows Jh, Gᵀ, Jhᵀ, G lights up as the learner hovers. Structural forces: a stiff linkage where some squeeze needs no joint torque (purple tension glow). Final beat: a 2×2 gallery of hands (closure yes/no × manipulable yes/no) with the 🛡️ and 🔀 badges.

scenes.title: SCARA Pinch
scenes.brief: Top-down + perspective view of two SCARA arms (orange joints, slate bases S1, S2) pinching a blue box at height a with soft fingertips. Sliders for l1, l2, r, b. Panels: G (from the box example), B, the SCARA Jacobian columns as twist arrows, and the adjoint into each contact frame. Composing them fills Jh block by block. Then the learner tries to drag the box: lifting and sliding work, but tipping it about the y-axis is impossible (coral, the needed column is not in range Jh). Finally the last revolute joint of each finger spins while the box stays still: internal motion, orange spin rings.

scenes.title: Surface Charts
scenes.brief: Left: a flat teal (u, v) grid patch with a draggable gold dot. Right: the same grid wrapped onto a 3D surface (sphere, cylinder, saddle, torus selectable). At the image dot: orange tangent arrows c_u and c_v, their lengths shown as bars (metric M), the blue unit normal n. Moving the dot shows n tilting: the tilt rate along each direction is the curvature K (two bars, zero on a flat sheet). A small RGB Gauss frame (x along c_u, y along c_v, z = n) rides along a drawn path; its twist about n is the torsion T (spin readout). The induced contact-frame velocity (Lemma 5.10) is shown as linear and angular arrows. Sphere example: radius slider, K = (1/ρ)I, M = diag(ρ, ρ cos u), and T grows near the poles.

scenes.title: Rolling Contact
scenes.brief: Two smooth bodies (pink finger surface F on top, blue object O below; sphere, ellipsoid, plane, saddle selectable) touching at one teal point. Both surfaces carry their (u, v) grid charts in small inset maps where a teal dot marks the contact coordinates α_f and α_o, and a dial shows the contact angle ψ between the two u-directions. The learner drives the relative motion with three orange rolling/spin knobs (ωx, ωy, ωz) and, in sliding mode, two sliding knobs (vx, vy); vz is locked at 0 (coral). As the finger rolls, the contact dots crawl across both inset maps exactly as the contact equations predict (integrated with RK4), leaving teal trails, while ψ turns. A relative-curvature meter (Kf + K̃o) shows its smallest eigenvalue; for a ball in a matching bowl it hits 0, the inset dot jumps wildly and a coral ⚠️ flashes. Proof beat: two frame paths (via Lf and via Co) to the same frame Cf, drawn as two gold routes that must give the same twist. Final beat: ball on a table, contact trails on the table (straight) and on the ball (curving, spinning faster near the poles).

scenes.title: Rolling Grasp
scenes.brief: Two round fingertips (pink spheres on orange-jointed fingers) hold a blue ellipsoid. As the object turns, the teal contact points roll to new places and the columns of G and the blocks of Jh visibly change (matrix panels animate their numbers). A clock icon integrates η̇ = A(η)V step by step (RK4); a drift meter compares integrated vs. true contact positions and grows slowly (purple), until a 📡 sensor ping snaps them back. A side panel maps contact coordinates η ↔ relative pose and shows the map is one-to-one while the relative curvature is invertible. The contact frame is built from the chart: unit tangent arrows (c_u/‖c_u‖, c_v/‖c_v‖) and the normal stacked into R, with the contact point as p.

scenes.title: Grasp Recap
scenes.brief: A single summary board: a blue object pinched by two orange-jointed fingers. Five tiles along the bottom; tapping one replays a ten-second clip from its scene: lime friction cones at the contacts, arrows flowing into G at the center, a coral shove cancelled (🛡️), the velocity/force diagram with Jh, Gᵀ, Jhᵀ, G, a fingertip rolling with its contact dot crawling across a chart.

scenes.title: Grasp Gym
scenes.brief: Challenge mode across the chapter scenes. Each card loads a shape, contacts and a goal; the learner must make the picture do the thing: place contacts until the 🛡️ badge lights, write a basis by dragging arrows until the allowed-force region matches a line or patch contact, design a shape that defeats a given number of fingers, paint the force-closure region on the edge-pair square, drag finger joints to show a grasp is (not) manipulable, or roll a fingertip so its contact dot follows a gold path. A lime ✓ appears only when the live computation confirms the answer.

pages.summary: Chapter opener: the hand–object kinematics problem, and why a big arm with a simple gripper is clumsy for fine work and limited in what it can hold.

atoms.idea: Chapter 5 title: kinematics of hands with several fingers.
The chapter links finger motions and forces to object motions and forces, asks when a grasp can manipulate an object, and treats fingers that stay put as well as fingers that roll or slide.
atoms.feynman: Carrying a tray with friends: how hard each person pushes and where they stand decides whether the tray goes where you want.
atoms.visual: Road-map strip of emoji tiles (📍 contact → 🗺️ grasp map → 🛡️ closure → 🧭 planning → 🦾 finger kinematics → ⚽ rolling); the tile for this scene glows gold.

atoms.idea: Section 5.1 heading: introduction to grasping.

An industrial arm with a simple gripper is good for large payload moves but poor at precise small motions, because tiny joint errors are amplified by long links; like writing by swinging your whole arm.
atoms.feynman: Try writing your name holding the pen with your shoulder only: the letters wobble. Use your fingers and they come out neat.
atoms.visual: Long slate arm with orange joints; purple jitter on each joint; the pink pen tip trace around a gold star wobbles a lot. Swap to a small hand on the same frozen arm: trace error bar (coral) drops sharply.

atoms.idea: A given gripper can only hold a narrow family of shapes (a parallel jaw likes parallel faces, not a tetrahedron); tool changers swap grippers to widen that family.
atoms.feynman: A clothes peg grips a flat card easily but cannot hold a marble or a pyramid.
atoms.visual: A parallel-jaw gripper tries a cube, a pyramid and a ball in turn: cube gets a lime ✓, the others slip out with a coral ✗; a 🔧 tool rack spins to swap jaws.

atoms.idea: Page number 211.

pages.summary: Multifingered hands as small robots mounted on an arm: better accuracy and more graspable shapes, at the price of contact constraints and harder planning.

atoms.feynman: A robot hand looks like your own hand: several jointed fingers sharing one palm.
atoms.visual: Stylized hand: a slate palm with four fingers drawn as orange-jointed chains; tapping a finger wiggles its joints.

atoms.idea: Tool changers widen the set of liftable objects but do nothing for fine motion.
atoms.feynman: Owning many cookie cutters lets you cut many shapes, but it does not make your hand steadier.
atoms.visual: The tool rack from the previous beat keeps spinning, yet the pen-tip wobble readout stays high: coral bar unchanged.

atoms.idea: A multifingered hand is a set of small robots attached to an arm; being small it adds accuracy, and its extra freedoms let one end-effector grasp many shapes.
atoms.feynman: Your arm brings your hand near the cup; your fingers do the delicate part.
atoms.visual: The hand explodes into its fingers, each shown as a mini arm with orange joints, then snaps back onto the arm tip; the cube, pyramid and ball now all get lime ✓.

atoms.idea: The cost: many degrees of freedom, contact constraints between hand and object in kinematics and dynamics, and a hard grasp-planning problem.
atoms.feynman: More fingers means more things to coordinate, like a team rowing a boat versus one person paddling.
atoms.visual: Counter badge of degrees of freedom climbs as fingers are added; purple constraint links appear between fingertips and the object; a gold question mark hovers over "where to touch".

atoms.idea: Hands are not a universal answer: custom tools solve many factory and transport jobs well.
atoms.feynman: A bottle opener beats fingers at opening bottles.
atoms.visual: Side-by-side: a custom fixture holds a part rigidly (lime) while the hand needs constant correction (purple jitter).

pages.summary: Custom tools are rigid by design, but hand ideas generalize to cooperating robots; overview of kinematics/planning versus dynamics/control and the two desirable grasp properties.

atoms.idea: A custom end-effector is stiff by construction while a fingered grasp needs feedback and is less rigid; still, hand theory covers coordinated multi-robot lifting, since two big robots act like two fingers.
atoms.feynman: Two movers carrying a sofa are just a giant two-finger hand.
atoms.visual: Zoom out from the hand: its two fingers morph into two full robot arms carrying one long gold box; the same contact arrows stay on the box.

atoms.idea: Subheading: overview of the chapter.
The study splits into kinematics/planning (this chapter) and dynamics/control (next), with new tools such as grasp planning and rolling kinematics.
atoms.feynman: Learning to juggle: first where the balls go, then how hard to throw.
atoms.visual: Road-map strip splits into two rows: this chapter (📍🗺️🛡️🧭⚽) and the next (⚙️🎛️).

atoms.idea: Kinematics: given object, finger and contact models with known contact locations and no slipping, find the force and velocity relations; this yields the basic grasping constraint.
atoms.feynman: If you know exactly where your fingertips touch a cup, you can work out how the cup moves when your fingers move.
atoms.visual: Teal contact dots on a blue object linked by purple constraint springs to pink fingertips; moving an orange finger joint drags the object along.

atoms.idea: Grasp planning picks contact locations; first we list what a good grasp should do.
atoms.feynman: Before picking up a bag, you decide where to put your hands.
atoms.visual: Gold candidate spots blink on the object outline; two wish-icons fade in.

atoms.idea: Property 1, force-closure: contact forces can produce a wrench opposing any external wrench on the object.
atoms.feynman: Holding a glass so firmly that nobody bumping it can knock it out of your hand.
atoms.visual: Random coral shove arrows hit the object; green-lime finger arrows instantly answer each one so the object stays still; 🛡️ icon glows.

atoms.idea: Property 2, manipulability: the fingers can produce whatever object motion the task needs, in all or some directions.
atoms.feynman: Holding a pencil so you can roll it, slide it, and tip it however you like.
atoms.visual: A gold target pose ghost; dragging it, the fingers follow and the object tracks it; 🔀 icon glows when every direction is reachable.

atoms.idea: Page number 213.

pages.summary: Wrap-up of the overview and assumptions (rigid bodies, exact models); start of grasp statics with fixed point contacts and contact coordinate frames.

atoms.idea: We choose contacts to achieve these properties where possible, shown via simple cases.
atoms.feynman: Trying a few hand positions on a box until one feels secure.
atoms.visual: Gold candidate spots on the outline; each placement lights 🛡️ and 🔀 in lime or coral.

atoms.idea: Preview: the next chapter extends arm dynamics to contact-constrained systems so that arm control laws carry over to hands, including redundant ones.
atoms.feynman: Once you can steer a bike, steering a tandem uses the same rules, just with two riders.
atoms.visual: Road-map tile ⚙️ for the dynamics chapter glows; the arm control-law icon slides onto the hand icon.

atoms.idea: Standing assumptions: rigid object and rigid fingers, and accurate models of both; relaxing them is research.
atoms.feynman: We pretend the cup is glass, not a squishy paper cup, so the math stays clean.
atoms.visual: Object rendered as hard blue block; a toggle to "squishy" shows purple wobble and a 🚧 sign.

atoms.idea: Section 5.2 heading: grasp statics.
Start simple: contacts are points at fixed places (no rolling or sliding), and finger kinematics is ignored; we only track how contact forces reach the object.
atoms.feynman: Think only about where your fingertips press a book, not how your knuckles bend.
atoms.visual: Fingers fade to ghosts; only teal contact dots and their orange push arrows remain on the blue object.

atoms.idea: Subsection 5.2.1 heading: contact models.

A contact model maps finger force at the contact to the wrench at a reference point on the object, always chosen as the center of mass; each contact and the object get frames, and contact locations are fixed on the object.
atoms.feynman: Pushing a door near the hinge or far from it: the same push makes a different turning effect at the hinge.
atoms.visual: Gold center-of-mass dot with RGB frame O; teal contact dot with its own frame Cᵢ; dragging the contact around the outline updates a wrench readout at O.

atoms.idea: Convention: each contact frame has its z-axis along the inward surface normal.
atoms.feynman: Your fingertip pushes straight into the surface: that inward direction is "z".
atoms.visual: The contact frame snaps so its blue z-arrow points into the object, re-orienting as the dot slides around a curved outline.

atoms.idea: Page number 214.

pages.summary: Contact frame placement g_oci, object pose g_po, and the frictionless point contact that can only push along the normal (Eq 5.1).

atoms.label: Fig 5.2
atoms.idea: Fig 5.2: palm frame P, object frame O and contact frame Cᵢ, linked by the transforms g_po and g_oci.
atoms.feynman: Three stickers with little compasses: one on the table, one on the cup, one at your fingertip.
atoms.visual: 3D: slate palm frame P, blue object with frame O, teal contact frame Cᵢ; gold arrows g_po and g_oci chain them; drag the object and both arrows update.

atoms.idea: The contact location is g_oci = (p_oci, R_oci) ∈ SE(3), converting contact coordinates into object coordinates; the object pose is x_o = g_po; a contact applies a wrench F_ci at its frame origin.
atoms.feynman: A map pin (where) with a compass (which way) says exactly where the fingertip sits on the cup.
atoms.visual: Hover g_oci: a point drawn in Cᵢ coordinates jumps to its O coordinates (teal numbers change, point does not move).

atoms.idea: Fingers cannot push in every direction; a few contact models classify this, starting from normal-only pushes and then adding friction.
atoms.feynman: A finger on ice can only press; a finger on sandpaper can also drag sideways.
atoms.visual: Mode switch chips: 🧊 (frictionless), 🍦 (friction), 🌀 (soft); the allowed-force region on the contact changes shape.

atoms.label: Eq (5.1)
atoms.idea: Frictionless point contact: F_ci = (0,0,1,0,0,0)·f_ci with f_ci ≥ 0: a pure push along the normal, no pulling.
atoms.feynman: A finger on a greased ball: you can only push it, you cannot pull it or drag it sideways.
atoms.visual: Drag the orange force arrow anywhere: only its inward-normal part survives as a lime arrow; if the drag points outward the arrow turns coral and vanishes (f < 0 forbidden).

atoms.idea: Page number 215.

pages.summary: Frictionless contacts as a conservative model; Coulomb friction |f_t| ≤ μ f_n (Eq 5.2) and the friction cone of half-angle atan μ.

atoms.label: Fig 5.3
atoms.idea: Fig 5.3: frictionless point contact: a single normal force at the contact.
atoms.feynman: Pressing a soap bar on wet tiles: only the straight-in push sticks.
atoms.visual: Blue object, teal dot, a single lime arrow along the inward normal; any tilt of the arrow is shed as coral.

atoms.idea: Frictionless contacts rarely occur but model low or unknown friction; using them guarantees a plan never relies on friction.
atoms.feynman: Planning to carry a tray as if it were slippery: if it works then, it works on any day.
atoms.visual: Toggle "trust friction" off: the cone collapses to a line; a plan that still holds gets a lime 🛡️.

atoms.idea: Coulomb friction: the tangential force a contact can sustain is proportional to the normal force, with a material-dependent constant.
atoms.feynman: The harder you press a book on a table, the harder you must shove to slide it.
atoms.visual: Press slider (normal force) and shove slider (tangential); a meter shows the allowed shove growing in proportion to the press.

atoms.label: Eq (5.2)
atoms.idea: Slip starts when |f_t| > μ f_n; so the allowed tangential range is |f_t| ≤ μ f_n (Eq 5.2), which needs f_n > 0 for any nonzero tangential force.
atoms.feynman: An eraser on paper: push down and it can drag the paper; lift off and it just slides.
atoms.visual: Bar chart: lime band of width μ·fn around zero for f_t; shove beyond it and the teal contact dot starts sliding with a coral trail.

atoms.idea: Geometrically the allowed forces fill a cone around the normal: the friction cone, half-angle α = atan μ.
atoms.feynman: An ice-cream cone stuck into the surface: any push that fits inside the cone holds.
atoms.visual: 3D lime ice-cream cone on the contact; μ slider opens it; the half-angle readout α = atan μ updates.

atoms.idea: Page number 216.

pages.summary: Friction cone picture, typical μ < 1 (cone under 45°), and the wrench bases for point contact with friction (Eq 5.3) and soft-finger contact (Eq 5.4).

atoms.label: Fig 5.4
atoms.idea: Fig 5.4: the friction cone around the surface normal, side view with legs fn and μfn and angle α.
atoms.feynman: A party hat stood upright on the table: the hat is the set of safe pushes.
atoms.visual: Side-view triangle: vertical teal fn, horizontal μfn, slanted edge; angle α glows orange; dragging μ tilts the edge.

atoms.idea: Most μ are below 1, so friction cones are usually narrower than 45°.
atoms.feynman: Most surfaces are slippery-ish: you cannot push at a steep slant without slipping.
atoms.visual: Reference 45° ghost cone in slate; most material chips (🪵 🔩 🧴) give cones inside it, rubber 🛞 pokes outside.

atoms.label: Eq (5.3)
atoms.idea: Point contact with friction: three force components (two tangential, one normal) with basis picking the first three wrench slots; allowed set √(f1²+f2²) ≤ μ f3, f3 ≥ 0 (Eq 5.3).
atoms.feynman: Your fingertip on a table can press down and also drag forward-back and left-right, as long as the drag is small compared to the press.
atoms.visual: The orange arrow can now point anywhere inside the lime cone; a 3-number readout (f1, f2, f3) with a gauge comparing √(f1²+f2²) to μf3.

atoms.label: Eq (5.4)
atoms.idea: Soft finger: adds a torque about the normal, bounded by torsional friction |f4| ≤ γ f3; the basis has four columns (Eq 5.4).
atoms.feynman: Press your thumb on a coin and twist: a soft pad can twist the coin a bit, a pin tip cannot.
atoms.visual: An orange twist ring around the normal axis; a small lime band |τ| ≤ γ·f3 shows how much twist is allowed; press harder and the band widens.

atoms.idea: Page number 217.

pages.summary: Friction-coefficient table, the general contact model (basis B_ci and cone FC_ci with two properties, Eq 5.5), and the first step of the grasp map: transforming a contact wrench to the object frame.

atoms.label: Table 5.1
atoms.idea: Table 5.1: static friction coefficients for common material pairs (metals around one half, wood a bit lower, rubber 1 to 4).
atoms.feynman: Rubber shoes grip a floor much better than socks: different pairs, different μ.
atoms.visual: Material chips (🔩 steel, 🪵 wood, 🧴 plastic, 👞 leather, 🛞 rubber) dropped on the contact; each sets μ and the lime cone visibly widens or narrows.

atoms.idea: General contact model: a wrench basis B_ci ∈ R^{p×m_i} (p = 6 in space, 3 in the plane; m_i independent force components) and a cone FC_ci that is closed with nonempty interior and closed under positive combinations.
atoms.feynman: Any mix of two safe pushes is still a safe push, like mixing two shades of green paint still gives green.
atoms.visual: Two lime arrows inside the cone; a slider mixes them with positive weights; the blended arrow stays lime (cone is closed under positive mixing).

atoms.label: Eq (5.5)
atoms.idea: Allowed contact wrenches: F_ci = B_ci f_ci with f_ci ∈ FC_ci (Eq 5.5); other models such as line and face contacts are left to exercises.
atoms.feynman: A recipe card (B) times a shopping list (f) gives the push you deliver.
atoms.visual: Matrix B shown as its column arrows; the f vector inside the cone scales them; the tip-to-tail sum is the delivered wrench.

atoms.idea: Subsection 5.2.2 heading: the grasp map.
To see a contact force from the object frame, multiply by the wrench transform Adᵀ of g_oci⁻¹: block matrix [R 0; p̂R R] applied to B_ci f_ci.
atoms.feynman: Pushing a merry-go-round at its edge: the push stays the same size at the center, but it also becomes a spin.
atoms.visual: An orange push at a teal contact; a ghost copy glides to the gold center and sprouts a curling torque arrow p × f; the 6-number wrench readout updates.

atoms.idea: The wrench transform maps contact wrenches to object wrenches; the contact map G_i = Adᵀ_{g_oci⁻¹} B_ci sends contact force coordinates to the object wrench.
atoms.feynman: A translator turns your fingertip language into the object’s language.
atoms.visual: G_i panel: its columns drawn as arrows at the center, each one the image of a basis arrow at the contact; hovering a column highlights its source.
atoms.beat: 🔁 carry a push to the center

atoms.idea: Page number 218.

pages.summary: Table of common contact types and the grasp map: the net wrench is the sum of contact-map outputs, G = [G1 … Gk] (Eq 5.6), F_o = G f_c (Eq 5.7).

atoms.label: Table 5.2
atoms.idea: Table 5.2: frictionless point (one normal column, f1 ≥ 0), point with friction (three columns, circular cone), soft finger (four columns, cone plus twist bound).
atoms.feynman: Three kinds of fingertip: a greased pin, a rubber pin, a soft rubber pad.
atoms.visual: Three contact cards side by side, each showing its basis columns as arrows and its allowed set (ray, cone, cone + twist band); clicking one swaps the active contact.

atoms.idea: With k fingers, the total wrench is the sum of each finger’s object wrench (all in the same frame); the map from all contact forces to it is the grasp map G: R^m → R^p, m = Σ m_i.

pages.summary: Force-closure: a grasp that can cancel any external wrench while keeping finger forces inside their cones (Def 5.2, Prop 5.1); internal forces as squeezes that produce zero net wrench (Def 5.3).

atoms.idea: Section 5.3 heading: force-closure.
A key grasp property is balancing external wrenches (e.g. gravity when lifting) with finger forces, while every finger force stays in its friction cone so nothing slips.
atoms.feynman: Holding a full shopping bag: your fingers must push up against gravity without the handle sliding out.
atoms.visual: A gold weight 🧲 pulls the blue object down (coral arrow); finger arrows inside lime cones tilt to push it back up; any arrow leaving its cone turns coral and the finger slides.

atoms.idea: Subsection 5.3.1 heading: formal definition.
A grasp that can resist every applied wrench is called force-closure.
atoms.feynman: A grip nobody can knock loose, whichever way they bump it.
atoms.visual: The 🛡️ badge appears above the object, waiting to be earned.

atoms.label: Def 5.2
atoms.idea: Def 5.2: a grasp is force-closure if for every external wrench F_e there are contact forces f_c ∈ FC with G f_c = −F_e.
atoms.feynman: Whatever bump you get, your fingers have an answer that exactly cancels it.
atoms.visual: Drag a coral shove wrench (arrow + torque dial) anywhere; the solver finds lime finger forces in the cones whose pink net wrench is its mirror image; the object stays perfectly still.

atoms.label: Prop 5.1
atoms.idea: Prop 5.1: a grasp is force-closure exactly when the image of the cone under G is all of wrench space, G(FC) = R^p.
atoms.feynman: If the set of pushes you can make fills every direction, you can fight any bump.
atoms.visual: Sample many f_c in FC and map them through G: a pink cloud in wrench space; it swells to fill the whole box (lime) or leaves a coral empty region.

atoms.idea: Internal forces are contact forces giving zero net wrench; in the planar rectangle example, pressing both normals equally, f_N = (0,1,0,1), gives G f_N = 0.
atoms.feynman: Squeezing a sandwich between your palms: you push hard, but the sandwich does not move.
atoms.visual: The two fingers on the rectangle press inward with equal lime arrows; the net-wrench meter reads exactly 0 while a squeeze gauge rises.

atoms.label: Def 5.3
atoms.idea: Def 5.3: an internal force is in the null space of G and in FC; strictly internal if it lies in the interior of FC.
atoms.feynman: A squeeze that stays safely inside every finger’s no-slip zone, not touching the edge.
atoms.visual: Null-space arrow f_N drawn beside G; each finger’s arrow shown inside its cone; a halo marks “strictly inside” when no arrow touches a cone wall.

atoms.idea: Terminology note: the literature says force-closure although wrench-closure would be more precise.
atoms.feynman: Calling it a “force” grip even though it also resists twisting.
atoms.visual: A tiny 🏷️ tag next to the 🛡️ badge flips between “force” and “wrench” icons (➡️ / 🌀).

atoms.idea: Page number 223.

pages.summary: Prop 5.2: force-closure iff G is onto and a strictly internal force exists, with its two-way proof; constructive conditions begin with frictionless grasps, where closure means columns positively span R^6.

atoms.idea: Internal forces let us push contact forces back inside the friction cones; existence of a strictly internal one is necessary for closure.
atoms.feynman: If your grip is slipping, squeeze harder: the extra squeeze changes nothing about the net push but makes the fingers stick.
atoms.visual: A finger arrow near the edge of its cone (orange-coral) rotates back toward the cone axis as the squeeze slider increases.

atoms.label: Prop 5.2
atoms.idea: Prop 5.2: force-closure ⇔ G is surjective and some f_N ∈ null(G) lies in the interior of FC.
atoms.feynman: Two needs: you can push in every direction (ignoring slip), and you have a squeeze that does nothing but tighten.
atoms.visual: Two checklist lights: 🗺️ “G reaches every direction” and 🤝 “strict squeeze exists”; both lime ⇒ 🛡️ lit.

atoms.label: Prop 5.2 proof
atoms.idea: Sufficiency: pick any f′ with G f′ = F_o; (f′ + α f_N)/α → f_N as α grows, so for large α the scaled vector is inside the cone; cones are closed under scaling, so f′ + α f_N ∈ int FC and still gives F_o.
atoms.feynman: Whatever wobbly grip gives the right push, add a giant squeeze: eventually the squeeze dominates and every finger sits snugly inside its cone, yet the push is unchanged.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) coral arrows f′ some outside cones, net wrench matches the gold target; (2) α slider grows, arrows f′ + α f_N lengthen and swing toward cone centers; (3) a shrink-view divides by α so they visibly converge to f_N; (4) all lime, net wrench readout unchanged.

atoms.label: Prop 5.2 proof
atoms.idea: Necessity: take an interior f1 with G f1 = F_o ≠ 0 and f2 ∈ FC with G f2 = −F_o; their sum is in null(G) and in the interior of FC.
atoms.feynman: A push and its exact opposite push, done at once, add up to pure squeezing.
atoms.visual: Two arrow sets: f1 (lime, interior) and f2 (lime); they merge into f_N; the net-wrench meter shows +F_o, −F_o, then 0.
atoms.beat: 🔁 proof back: two pushes make a squeeze

atoms.idea: Subsection 5.3.2 heading: constructive force-closure conditions.

Checking closure directly is hard because of cone shapes; for frictionless point contacts G has columns (n_i, p_i × n_i) and FC is the positive orthant, so closure means the columns positively span R^6.
atoms.feynman: With slippery fingertips, you only have a fixed set of arrows you may stretch forward but never reverse.
atoms.visual: Arrows = columns of G; each has a forward-only slider (no negative values); the lime reachable region grows as positive mixtures.

atoms.idea: Page number 224.

pages.summary: Positive linear algebra: positively dependent and positively spanning sets, convex sets and the convex hull (Fig 5.7a), and the start of separating hyperplanes.

atoms.label: Fig 5.7
atoms.idea: Fig 5.7: (a) the convex hull of six points; (b) a hyperplane separating a convex set from an outside point c.

atoms.idea: So force-closure becomes a question about positive linear combinations.
atoms.feynman: Instead of asking “can I push any way?”, ask “can forward-only arrows reach everywhere?”.
atoms.visual: Transition: finger arrows on the object fly to a common origin and become plain arrows in wrench space.

atoms.idea: Positively dependent: some combination with all coefficients strictly positive sums to zero.
atoms.feynman: A tug-of-war with ropes in many directions where everyone pulls and the knot stays still.
atoms.visual: Arrows with positive-only sliders; when a combination closes into a loop (tip-to-tail back to start) a gold ✓ appears.

atoms.idea: Positively spanning: every vector equals a strictly positive combination; such a set is automatically positively dependent (target 0), and coefficients must be strictly positive.
atoms.feynman: A team of ropes that can drag the knot to any spot on the field using only pulls.
atoms.visual: A gold target dot dragged anywhere; the sliders auto-solve for positive weights; if the target is unreachable the weight that would need to go negative flashes coral.

atoms.idea: Convex set: contains every segment between its points; convex hull co(S): the smallest convex set containing S, equal to all convex combinations Σα_i v_i, α_i ≥ 0, Σα_i = 1.
atoms.feynman: A rubber band around nails: everything inside the band is a blend of the nails.
atoms.visual: Drag a test point inside the blue hull: barycentric weights shown as teal bars summing to 1; outside the hull one bar turns coral (negative).

atoms.idea: Separating hyperplanes are the key tool for convex sets; they are defined next.
atoms.feynman: A fence that keeps a herd of sheep on one side.
atoms.visual: A slate fence line appears, ready to be rotated.

atoms.idea: Page number 225.

pages.summary: Separating and supporting hyperplanes; Prop 5.3 gives four equivalent tests for frictionless force-closure and a practical way to build candidate hyperplanes from columns; Ex 5.4 begins.

atoms.idea: Hyperplane through c with normal v: all x with vᵀ(x − c) = 0.
atoms.feynman: A flat wall standing at point c, facing direction v.
atoms.visual: A slate plane through a gold dot c with a normal arrow v; rotate v and the wall turns.

atoms.idea: For a convex set K and a point c outside it there is a hyperplane with all of K strictly on one side (separating); if c is on K’s boundary use ≥ (supporting).
atoms.feynman: Any pile of sand and a pebble outside it: you can always slide a sheet of paper between them.
atoms.visual: Drag c out of the hull: a separating wall auto-appears (coral) with every pin on the far side; drag c onto the hull’s edge: wall becomes a tangent (supporting) plane.

atoms.label: Prop 5.3
atoms.idea: Prop 5.3: for frictionless point grasps, equivalent: (1) force-closure; (2) columns of G positively span R^p; (3) their convex hull contains a neighborhood of the origin; (4) no nonzero v has v·G_i ≥ 0 for all columns.
atoms.feynman: Four ways to say the same thing: you can push any way; your arrows reach everywhere; their rubber band surrounds the center; no wall through the center has all arrows on one side.
atoms.visual: Four synchronized panels with one shared set of arrows: reachable region, hull bubble around gold origin, rotatable wall through origin, and the 🛡️ badge; dragging any arrow updates all four lights together.

atoms.idea: (1)⇔(2) is the definition for frictionless contacts; the rest rely on convex-analysis results not proved here.
atoms.feynman: Two of the four facts are just the definition said twice; the others are known geometry facts.
atoms.visual: Lights 🛡️ and ➕ linked with a solid lime chain; the other two linked by a dashed slate chain marked 📚.

atoms.idea: Condition 4 is easy to compute: build v perpendicular to any p−1 independent columns, then check whether the dot products with the remaining columns have mixed signs; only such v need checking; such a v is a supporting plane through the origin.
atoms.feynman: To see whether arrows all lean one way, lay a wall along some of them and look whether the rest fall on both sides.
atoms.visual: Button “try a wall”: a plane through the origin snaps to contain p−1 chosen arrows; the remaining arrow tips show + or − chips; all-same-sign chips turn coral (wall found ⇒ not closure).

atoms.label: Ex 5.4
atoms.idea: Ex 5.4: four planar contacts near the corners of a rectangle; G has rows (fx, fy, τ) with lever terms a, b > 0.
atoms.feynman: Four fingers poking a domino, each a little off-center.
atoms.visual: A blue rectangle with four inward arrows offset from the axes by sliders a and b; the four columns plotted as arrows in (fx, fy, τ).

pages.summary: Fig 5.8 and Ex 5.4 continued: all six candidate walls from column pairs show mixed signs, so the offset grasp is force-closure; with the offsets zeroed the torque row vanishes.

atoms.label: Fig 5.8

atoms.label: Ex 5.4
atoms.idea: Candidate walls v_ij perpendicular to columns i and j are listed with their dot products against all columns; every list has both signs, so condition 4 never fails and the grasp is force-closure.
atoms.feynman: Lay a wall along any two pokes; the other two pokes always land on opposite sides, so the pokes can’t all lean one way.
atoms.visual: Six wall buttons (v12…v34); each rotates the plane into place and shows four sign chips; every row shows one + and one −, lime; the 🛡️ badge lights.

atoms.feynman: Pushing through the center can never twist the domino.
atoms.visual: Slide a and b to 0: the τ coordinates of all four columns drop to the floor; the torque bar row turns to zeros.

atoms.label: Fig 5.9
atoms.idea: Fig 5.9: two frictional point contacts on opposite sides of a planar object, each cone drawn by its two edges, and the edge wrenches in (fx, fy, τ).
atoms.feynman: Each V-shaped no-slip zone is just its two edges; anything in between is a blend.
atoms.visual: Two lime V-wedges at the contacts, edges marked f⁺ and f⁻; the four edge rays plotted in wrench space with their hull.

atoms.feynman: Fingers poking at the center can push the domino around but can never hold it against a twist.
atoms.visual: Apply a coral torque dial to the centered grasp: the domino spins away; the wall v = τ-axis lights with all four chips showing 0.

atoms.label: Ex 5.5
atoms.idea: Ex 5.5: any force in a friction cone is a positive mix of the cone’s edge forces, so closure can be tested by checking whether the edge wrenches positively span wrench space.
atoms.feynman: A slice of pizza is all the blends of its two straight edges.
atoms.visual: Each V-wedge splits into its two edge arrows; sweeping a blend slider moves a lime arrow between them, always staying inside the wedge.

atoms.feynman: A rubber finger acts like two slippery fingers tilted to the cone edges.
atoms.visual: One frictional finger turns into two ghost frictionless fingers along the wedge edges; the convex-hull test from the previous beats runs unchanged.

pages.summary: Spatial friction cones approximated by pyramids (sufficient test); Section 5.4 grasp planning starts with how many contacts are needed.

atoms.label: Fig 5.10
atoms.idea: Fig 5.10: circular friction cones approximated by pyramids with finitely many edges.
atoms.feynman: Cutting a round ice-cream cone into a pyramid of flat faces that fits inside it.
atoms.visual: A lime circular cone with an inscribed teal pyramid; an edges slider (3, 4, 6, 8, 16) makes the pyramid hug the cone more closely.

atoms.idea: In 3D the round cone is not a finite sum of rays, so approximate it by an inscribed pyramid; if the hull of pyramid-edge wrenches contains the origin’s neighborhood, the grasp is force-closure (sufficient, not necessary).
atoms.feynman: If you can hold a glass using only a few safe directions, you can certainly hold it with all of them.
atoms.visual: Run the hull test with an inscribed pyramid: lime ⇒ closure guaranteed; coral ⇒ undecided (a ❔ badge), and adding more edges can flip it to lime.

atoms.idea: Section 5.4 heading: grasp planning.
This section sketches ways to choose contact points that give force-closure.
atoms.feynman: Deciding where to put your fingers before picking something up.
atoms.visual: Gold candidate dots blink around the outline of a shape.

atoms.idea: Subsection 5.4.1 heading: bounds on the number of required contacts.
Designing a hand starts with how many and what kind of fingers; given a contact type, how many are needed to grasp any object gives a lower bound.
atoms.feynman: How many chopsticks do you need to hold any snack?
atoms.visual: A finger counter (orange) beside a parade of shapes; the question mark tile hovers over the count.

atoms.idea: Let the object O have boundary Σ, assumed connected and piecewise smooth.
atoms.feynman: The skin of the object is what fingers can touch.
atoms.visual: Object outline glows teal: that is Σ.

atoms.idea: Page number 229.

pages.summary: Wrenches from frictionless contacts on a surface; exceptional surfaces (sphere, circle) cannot be grasped that way; Carathéodory (at least p+1) and Steinitz (at most 2p) bounds.

atoms.label: Fig 5.11
atoms.idea: Fig 5.11: three sets of plane vectors: one that fails to positively span R², and two four-vector sets that do.
atoms.feynman: Arrows on a compass: if they leave a gap, some direction cannot be reached.
atoms.visual: Three panels of arrows from the origin; a gold probe arrow sweeps around; in the failing panel a coral gap sector lights where the probe is unreachable.

atoms.idea: Λ(Σ) is the set of wrenches (n, p × n) from frictionless contacts anywhere on Σ; Σ is exceptional if the hull of Λ(Σ) misses a neighborhood of the origin; then no frictionless grasp exists; the circle and sphere are exceptional.
atoms.feynman: A perfectly slippery ball: every push goes through the middle, so nothing stops it from spinning.
atoms.visual: Click contacts on a disk: every wrench arrow lies flat (τ = 0) in the 3D plot, the hull is a pancake and the gold origin is never inside (coral 🚫); swap to an ellipse and the arrows gain τ and the hull inflates.

atoms.idea: For non-exceptional surfaces two classic convexity theorems bound the number of contacts.
atoms.feynman: Two old rules tell you the fewest and the most fingers you could ever need.
atoms.visual: Two orange ticks appear on the finger counter: a low one and a high one.

atoms.label: Thm 5.4
atoms.idea: Thm 5.4 (Carathéodory): a set that positively spans R^p has at least p+1 vectors.
atoms.feynman: To pull a knot anywhere on a table you need at least three ropes; two only work along a line.
atoms.visual: Try positively spanning the plane with 2 arrows: the region they reach is a wedge, the opposite direction −(v1+v2) is a coral unreachable gold target; add a third arrow and the wedge closes into the full plane.

atoms.label: Thm 5.5
atoms.idea: Thm 5.5 (Steinitz): if q is interior to the hull of S ⊂ R^p, then at most 2p points of S already have q in the interior of their hull.
atoms.feynman: From a big crowd surrounding you, you can always pick at most 2p people who still surround you.
atoms.visual: Big cloud of teal points around a gold q; a “prune” button removes points one by one while q stays inside; it ends with at most 2p (4 in the plane) points.

atoms.idea: Carathéodory means any force-closure grasp has at least p+1 contacts: with two vectors in the plane, −(v_i + v_j) is never reachable; more than p+1 vectors may still fail to span.
atoms.feynman: Two people pulling a sled can’t pull it backward against both of them.
atoms.visual: Pick any two arrows: gold target −(vi+vj) blinks coral; a three-arrow set with a gap (left panel of Fig 5.11) still fails.

atoms.idea: Steinitz gives the upper bound: set S = Λ(Σ), q = 0.
atoms.feynman: Now count the most fingers you could possibly need.
atoms.visual: The prune animation starts on the wrench cloud of a shape’s boundary.

atoms.idea: Page number 230.

pages.summary: Table 5.3 of contact-count bounds; Steinitz gives at most 2p contacts; frictionless bounds 4–6 (plane), 7–12 (space) with known achievable cases; frictional cases need fewer.

atoms.label: Table 5.3
atoms.idea: Table 5.3: minimum contacts by space (planar/spatial), object class (exceptional, non-exceptional, polyhedral) and contact type: frictionless 4 or 7 (12 for general smooth 3D bodies), friction or soft 3 (plane) or 4 (space).
atoms.feynman: A recipe card: slippery fingers need many, sticky fingers need few.
atoms.visual: Emoji grid: rows 🟦 plane / 🧊 space × object type; columns 🧈 frictionless, 🍦 friction, 🌀 soft; each cell shows a count with that many finger icons.

atoms.idea: By Steinitz, a non-exceptional object needs at most 2p frictionless contacts; the choice is not unique and some members may be redundant.
atoms.feynman: Among many good finger spots, you can always throw some away and keep at most 2p.
atoms.visual: Two four-arrow sets spanning the plane: in one, hiding any arrow breaks it (all needed); in the other, one arrow can be hidden without loss (redundant, dimmed).

atoms.idea: Frictionless bounds: plane (p = 3) 4 ≤ k ≤ 6; space (p = 6) 7 ≤ k ≤ 12.
atoms.feynman: Slippery fingers: 4 to 6 for a flat cut-out, 7 to 12 for a solid toy.
atoms.visual: Finger counter with orange ticks at p+1 and 2p for p = 3 and p = 6.

atoms.idea: In the plane the lower bound 4 is always achievable for non-exceptional shapes; in space, 7 suffice for some classes (polyhedra, everywhere-smooth bodies) but not proven in general.
atoms.feynman: For flat shapes four slippery fingers always suffice; for 3D, seven work for boxes and smooth pebbles.

atoms.idea: Thm 5.9: every regular surface has a local orthogonal chart (standard differential geometry).

atoms.label: Eq (5.17)
atoms.idea: First fundamental form I_p: the 2×2 Gram matrix [c_uᵀc_u, c_uᵀc_v; c_vᵀc_u, c_vᵀc_v] (Eq 5.17), giving inner products and areas of tangent vectors.
atoms.feynman: How much a map stretches: a centimetre on the map may be a kilometre near the equator but less near the poles.
atoms.visual: A unit square on the flat grid maps to a parallelogram on the surface; its area readout = √det I_p; the 2×2 matrix entries pulse as the dot moves.

atoms.idea: I_p is symmetric positive definite; for orthogonal charts it is diagonal.
atoms.feynman: Stretch is never negative.
atoms.visual: Off-diagonal entries fade to 0 when the right-angle marker is lime.

atoms.label: Eq (5.18)
atoms.idea: Metric tensor M_p: the positive definite square root of I_p; for orthogonal charts M_p = diag(‖c_u‖, ‖c_v‖) (Eq 5.18).
atoms.feynman: The stretch factor in each map direction.
atoms.visual: Two orange bars show ‖c_u‖ and ‖c_v‖; on a globe the v-bar shrinks toward the poles.

atoms.idea: An outward unit normal is built from the cross product of the tangent vectors.
atoms.feynman: The direction a hair grows out of your head.
atoms.visual: A blue normal arrow appears as c_u × c_v.

pages.summary: Gauss map (Eq 5.19), second fundamental form (Eq 5.20), curvature tensor K (Eq 5.21), and the normalized Gauss frame (Eq 5.22–5.23).

atoms.label: Eq (5.19)
atoms.idea: Gauss map N: surface → unit sphere, N = c_u × c_v / ‖c_u × c_v‖ (Eq 5.19); smooth for smooth orientable surfaces.
atoms.feynman: Paint each spot of a balloon with the direction its hair points; collect those directions on a reference ball.
atoms.visual: Side inset: a small unit sphere; as the gold dot moves on the surface, a matching dot moves on the inset sphere at the normal’s direction.

atoms.label: Eq (5.20)
atoms.idea: Second fundamental form II_p = [c_uᵀn_u, c_uᵀn_v; c_vᵀn_u, c_vᵀn_v] (Eq 5.20): how fast the normal turns, projected on the tangent plane; along an arc-length curve p′ᵀ II p′ gives its normal curvature.
atoms.feynman: Walking over a hill: how fast your “up” direction tilts per step is the bend of the hill.
atoms.visual: Move the dot one step along c_u: the blue normal tilts; the tilt arrow n_u projected on the tangent card is drawn orange; its size feeds the II_p entries.

atoms.label: Eq (5.21)
atoms.idea: Curvature tensor K_p = M⁻ᵀ II M⁻¹ (Eq 5.21): the second form normalized for chart stretching.
atoms.feynman: Bending per real centimetre, not per map unit.
atoms.visual: Two curvature bars (K entries); scaling the chart (stretching the grid) changes II but leaves K’s bars unchanged.

atoms.label: Eq (5.22)
atoms.idea: Normalized Gauss frame [x y z] = [c_u/‖c_u‖, c_v/‖c_v‖, n] (Eq 5.22), an orthonormal frame at each point.
atoms.feynman: A tiny compass glued flat to the surface, with one needle sticking out.
atoms.visual: Small RGB frame on the dot: red along c_u, green along c_v, blue = normal.

atoms.label: Eq (5.23)
atoms.idea: In the Gauss frame, K = [xᵀ; yᵀ][n_u/‖c_u‖, n_v/‖c_v‖] (Eq 5.23): how the unit normal varies, projected on the tangent plane.
atoms.feynman: How quickly the stick of the compass tilts as you slide the compass.
atoms.visual: Slide the frame: the blue axis tilts; its rate in the red and green directions fills K’s 2×2 cells.

pages.summary: Flat surfaces have K = 0; the torsion form T (Eq 5.24); the geometric parameters (M, K, T); the contact frame moving along a curve (Fig 5.19) and Lemma 5.10 begins.

atoms.label: Eq (5.24)
atoms.idea: Torsion form T_p = yᵀ[x_u/‖c_u‖, x_v/‖c_v‖] (Eq 5.24), a row vector measuring how the Gauss frame spins about the normal as you move; related to Christoffel symbols; zero on flat surfaces.
atoms.feynman: Walking along latitude lines near the North Pole, your map-north arrow swings around even though you walk “straight”.
atoms.visual: Move the frame along v near a sphere’s pole: the red and green axes spin about the blue normal; a spin-rate readout = T·(step); on a plane it reads 0.

atoms.idea: (M, K, T) are the geometric parameters: local stretch, bending and twisting, which drive contact kinematics.
atoms.feynman: Three numbers about the ground under your shoe: how stretched the map is, how curved, how twisty.
atoms.visual: Three gauges side by side (📏 M, 🧭 K, 🔄 T) updating live under the dot.

atoms.idea: For a curve p(t) in one chart with local coordinates α(t), define the contact frame C as the Gauss frame at p(t); its motion g_oc(t) is to be found from the geometric parameters.

atoms.visual: Learner drags the gold dot in (u, v); the frame trail on the surface leaves ghost copies; g_oc readout updates.

atoms.label: Lemma 5.10
atoms.idea: Lemma 5.10: v_oc = (M α̇, 0) (Eq 5.25) and ω_oc has spin T M α̇ about the normal and tilt K M α̇ in the tangent plane (Eq 5.26).

atoms.label: Lemma 5.10 proof
atoms.idea: Proof part 1: position is c(α(t)) and rotation is the Gauss frame; body linear velocity Rᵀ ṗ = [x y z]ᵀ c_α α̇ = (M α̇, 0) since z ⟂ tangents.

atoms.label: Lemma 5.10 proof
atoms.idea: Proof part 2: body angular velocity Rᵀ Ṙ is skew with entries xᵀẏ, xᵀż, yᵀż; these are identified with T M α̇ and K M α̇.
atoms.feynman: How the compass turns is read off from how each needle changes, measured against the other needles.

atoms.idea: Subsection 5.6.2 heading: contact kinematics.
Two bodies with surfaces S_o, S_f touch at a point; how do the contact points move over each surface as the bodies move relative to each other?
atoms.feynman: Roll one marble on another: the touching spot wanders over both marbles.
atoms.visual: Pink finger body on blue object; teal contact point; inset charts of both surfaces show the contact dot.

atoms.idea: Let p_o(t), p_f(t) be the contact points in each body frame, with orthogonal charts and local coordinates α_o, α_f; the contact angle ψ is the angle between the u-tangents of the two charts at the contact, signed about the outward normal of S_o.
atoms.feynman: Two maps laid face to face at a pin: how much one map is rotated relative to the other is ψ.
atoms.visual: Inset dial: the orange u-arrow of S_o and the pink u-arrow of S_f at the contact, the angle between them shaded gold = ψ.

pages.summary: Contact coordinates η = (α_f, α_o, ψ); the contact set W; contact and local frames; relative motion split into rolling (ωx, ωy), spinning (ωz) and sliding (vx, vy), with vz = 0 in contact.

atoms.label: Fig 5.21
atoms.idea: Fig 5.21: two bodies touching, with the u-tangent of each surface at the contact and the angle ψ between them.
atoms.feynman: Two spinning tops touching nose to nose.
atoms.visual: Pink and blue bodies, teal contact, two u-arrows and the gold ψ arc; rotate F about the normal and ψ changes.

atoms.idea: The contact coordinates η = (α_f, α_o, ψ) collect where the contact is on each body and the relative twist angle.
atoms.feynman: Three facts: where on my finger, where on the cup, how rotated.
atoms.visual: A five-number readout (2 + 2 + 1) beside the insets.

atoms.idea: g_of is the relative pose of F with respect to O; we restrict to the set W of poses where the bodies touch.
atoms.feynman: Of all the ways to place your finger, only the touching ones count.
atoms.visual: Free-drag the finger: whenever it lifts off or sinks in, the pose turns coral; the lime sheet of touching poses is W.

atoms.idea: Contact frames C_o, C_f follow the Gauss frames at the moving contact points; local frames L_o(τ), L_f(τ) are body-fixed copies that coincide with them at time τ.
atoms.feynman: A footprint left in the sand where your foot was a moment ago.
atoms.visual: At each instant, ghost frames (L) are stamped on both bodies where the moving contact frames (C) currently are; the C frames move on, leaving a trail of stamps.

atoms.idea: Relative motion of L_f to L_o: ωx, ωy are rolling, ωz spin about the normal, vx, vy sliding, vz normal (zero while in contact); pure rolling: vx = vy = ωz = 0; pure sliding: ω = 0.
atoms.feynman: A ball can roll (tip over), spin like a top, or skid; staying on the floor means never moving up or down.
atoms.visual: Six knobs: two orange roll knobs, one orange spin knob, two teal slide knobs, one coral locked vz; mode chips “roll only” and “slide only” lock the others.

pages.summary: Relative velocity of the local frames as an adjoint of V_of (Eq 5.27); rotation R_ψ, curvature K̃_o seen from C_f, relative curvature K_f + K̃_o; Theorem 5.11 the contact equations (Eq 5.28).

atoms.label: Fig 5.22
atoms.idea: Fig 5.22: the family of body-fixed local frames L_o(τ) along the moving contact, coinciding with C_o at time t.
atoms.feynman: Stepping stones dropped where the contact passes.
atoms.visual: A row of ghost frames along the teal trail on the blue body; the current one glows and coincides with the moving contact frame.

atoms.label: Eq (5.27)
atoms.idea: V_{lo lf} = Ad⁻¹_{g_f lf} V_of (Eq 5.27): the relative body twist re-expressed at the contact, components (vx, vy, vz, ωx, ωy, ωz).
atoms.feynman: The same motion described from right at the touching spot.
atoms.visual: Twist arrows of F relative to O hop to the contact frame; six component bars appear under the knobs.

atoms.idea: R_ψ (a reflection-rotation by ψ) relates the tangent axes of C_f and C_o; K̃_o = R_ψ K_o R_ψ is the object curvature in the finger’s axes; K_f + K̃_o is the relative curvature form.
atoms.feynman: How sharply the two surfaces curve away from each other at the touching point.
atoms.visual: Two curvature ellipses (pink K_f and blue K̃_o rotated by ψ) add into a gold relative-curvature ellipse.

atoms.label: Thm 5.11
atoms.idea: Thm 5.11 (contact equations): α̇_f = M_f⁻¹ (K_f + K̃_o)⁻¹ ((−ωy, ωx) − K̃_o (vx, vy)); α̇_o = M_o⁻¹ R_ψ (K_f + K̃_o)⁻¹ ((−ωy, ωx) + K_f (vx, vy)); ψ̇ = ωz + T_f M_f α̇_f + T_o M_o α̇_o; vz = 0 (Eq 5.28).
atoms.feynman: Roll a ball one way and its touching spot crawls in a predictable direction on both surfaces: tighter curves move the spot less.
atoms.visual: Turn the roll knobs: teal contact dots crawl across both inset charts at the predicted rates (RK4 integrated), ψ dial turns; a check overlay from brute-force geometry stays on top of the prediction.

pages.summary: The equations need invertible relative curvature (fails for a convex body in a matching concave one); proof of Thm 5.11: frame velocity bookkeeping (Eq 5.29–5.34).

atoms.idea: The contact equations need K_f + K̃_o invertible; it is singular e.g. for a convex body inside a concave one of the same radius, where tiny motions cause big contact jumps; we assume an open region where it is invertible.
atoms.feynman: A ball in a bowl of exactly its own size: nudge it and the touching spot could be anywhere.
atoms.visual: Bowl radius slider approaches the ball radius: the gold relative-curvature ellipse collapses to a line, the inset contact dot jitters wildly, coral ⚠️ flashes.

atoms.label: Eq (5.29)–(5.30)
atoms.idea: L_f is fixed to F so V_{f lf} = 0, hence V_{f cf} = V_{lf cf} (Eq 5.29); likewise V_{o co} = V_{lo co} (Eq 5.30).
atoms.feynman: A stepping stone doesn’t move with the bug, so the bug’s motion seen from the stone equals its motion seen from the ground.
atoms.visual: Staircase 1: frame F and stamped L_f share one color; their relative twist bar reads 0.

atoms.label: Eq (5.31)–(5.32)
atoms.idea: Compute the velocity of C_f relative to L_o by two routes: through L_f (Eq 5.31, coincident frames) and through C_o (Eq 5.32, rotated by R_{co cf}).
atoms.feynman: Two paths from home to the park must describe the same trip.
atoms.visual: Staircase 2: two gold routes L_o→L_f→C_f and L_o→C_o→C_f light up; their twist sums are shown side by side.

atoms.label: Eq (5.33)
atoms.idea: Combining gives one vector identity between the two routes (Eq 5.33).
atoms.feynman: Same trip, two descriptions, set equal.
atoms.visual: Staircase 3: an equals sign snaps between the two twist sums.

atoms.label: Eq (5.34)
atoms.idea: C_o and C_f share a point and differ by rotation R_ψ about the normal, so their relative twist is pure spin ψ̇ (Eq 5.34); V_{lo lf} is the six-component relative velocity.
atoms.feynman: The two compasses at the touching spot are stacked; one only turns relative to the other.
atoms.visual: Staircase 4: the two contact frames overlap; only a ψ̇ spin arrow around blue z remains.

pages.summary: Proof of Thm 5.11 finished using Lemma 5.10 on both surfaces (Eq 5.35–5.37); Corollary 5.11.1 for pure rolling (Eq 5.38); Example 5.7 sphere rolling on a plane begins.

atoms.label: Eq (5.35)–(5.36)
atoms.idea: Apply Lemma 5.10 to each surface: contact-frame velocities are (M α̇, 0) with angular parts from K M α̇ and T M α̇ (Eq 5.35–5.36).
atoms.feynman: Each surface’s compass moves by its own stretch, bend and twist rules.
atoms.visual: Staircase 5: both insets show their riding frames with linear/tilt/spin arrows, colored by surface (pink F, blue O).

atoms.label: Eq (5.37)
atoms.idea: Substituting and matching components gives linear relations (Eq 5.37) that rearrange into Eq (5.28).
atoms.feynman: Line up the two sides term by term and solve for how the touching spots move.
atoms.visual: Staircase 6: matched rows glow pairwise; solving collapses them into the three contact equations from the theorem beat (lime ✓).

atoms.idea: Grasping usually assumes rolling without slipping, which simplifies the equations.
atoms.feynman: Fingers usually roll on an object rather than skid.
atoms.visual: Mode chip “roll only” locks the slide knobs and the spin knob.

atoms.label: Cor 5.11.1
atoms.idea: Cor 5.11.1: pure rolling: α̇_f = M_f⁻¹(K_f+K̃_o)⁻¹(−ωy, ωx), α̇_o = M_o⁻¹ R_ψ (K_f+K̃_o)⁻¹(−ωy, ωx), ψ̇ = T_f M_f α̇_f + T_o M_o α̇o (Eq 5.38).

atoms.idea: Fig 5.24: palm, object, finger bases, contact and fingertip frames for moving contacts.

atoms.label: Eq (5.40)
atoms.idea: Same derivation as fixed contacts, but G and Jh depend on the contact coordinates η: Jh(θ, x_o, η) θ̇ = Gᵀ(η) V and η̇ᵢ = Aᵢ(ηᵢ) V_ofᵢ with Aᵢ ∈ R^{5×6} from Eq (5.28) (Eq 5.40); one extra fact, B_ciᵀ V_oc = 0, is left as an exercise.

atoms.label: Prop 5.12
atoms.idea: Prop 5.12: η ∈ R⁵ and touching relative pose g_of ∈ W are in smooth local one-to-one correspondence if K_f + R_ψᵀ K_o R_ψ is full rank.

atoms.label: Eq (5.41)
atoms.idea: Since η is a smooth function of the relative pose (and so of θ, x_o), the constraint becomes Jh(θ, x_o) θ̇ = Gᵀ(θ, x_o) V^b_po (Eq 5.41), extending Eq (5.15); all definitions and properties carry over.

atoms.idea: Computing η from pose is usually impractical, so use η directly; only Ad⁻¹ of g_oc varies with η (the other adjoint factors are fixed or depend on x_o).

atoms.visual: The chain S→P→O→C with only the last link (O→C) pulsing teal as η changes.

atoms.idea: Contact frame aligned with the object’s normalized Gauss frame: R_oc = [∂c/∂α M⁻¹, n], p_oc = c(α), giving g_oc (Eq 5.42).

atoms.idea: Section 5.7 heading: summary.
